title: cudaMallocAsync free-zone thrashing and KV-cache handshake causing transient resident growth
creator: Asha Patel
description: Symptom: long-running dedicated workers serving continuous-batched requests show periodic spikes in RSS/GPU resident memory followed by slow returns to baseline. The pattern correlates with heavy KV cache prefetches mixed with small, irregular batch sizes. Hypothesis: cudaMallocAsync arenas are being fragmented by a pattern of many small allocations and frees (the "free-zone thrash"), and the KV cache prefetch handoff uses allocation patterns that prevent timely coalescing of freed blocks. Resulting behavior is transient growth of resident device memory and longer lived arenas that are only returned much later by the async allocator, causing increased OOM risk under sustained load.
reproduction_steps: 1) Start a dedicated runtime node with KV cache enabled and prefetch=on, warm model to sequence length 1024.
2) Drive continuous-batching traffic with a 70/30 split of small (1-4 token) and medium (50-150 token) requests to simulate mixed workloads.
3) Instrument with nvml and runtime /proc/mem stats; enable allocator debug flags: ENV RUNTIME_ALLOC_DEBUG=1 and RUNTIME_CUDAASYNC_TRACE=1.
4) Observe GPU RSS/resident increase after large KV prefetch waves and sampling of cudaMallocAsync allocation timelines.
5) Capture allocator timeline and stream events (cupti traces optional) for a 30 minute window when spikes occur.
6) Repeat with prefetch disabled to validate KV handoff contribution.
7) Run with delayed-free trimming (experimental patch) to observe if coalescing changes spike amplitude/timing.
8) Record perf dashboard snapshots (latency, token throughput, device memory) for each experiment.
Notes: reproducer requires continuous-batching harness available in infra/canary/kv-prefetcher (internal).
investigation_notes: Initial sampling shows a recurring pattern where many small device allocations (~1-16KB) appear clustered around KV prefetch completion. These allocations are freed quickly but on different CUDA streams, leading to the allocator retaining multiple small slabs in separate arenas.

cudaMallocAsync returns pages to the device async free list but per-stream stream fences are delaying actual physical page returns; our implementation of KV cache handshake issues prefetches across streams without proper stream synchronization on free paths.
Observed ghost arenas: freed but still resident pages counted by nvml until host-side async release path completes; timeline indicates tens of seconds of delayed reclamation under peak throughput.
We see increased slab metadata churn when small allocation sizes dominate; slab freelist search cost and fragmentation increases (confirmed by allocator histogram sample).
Turning off prefetch reduces spikes by ~55% in the repro, suggesting KV handoff plays a major role. However some residual fragmentation remains from mixed-size continuous-batching.

Memory profiler snapshot: allocator reports many free blocks but fragmentation index remains high because freed blocks are spread across many small arenas instead of coalesced into large free extents.
Anecdotal: a canary with coalescing enabled (local debug build) shows quicker baseline recovery but marginally increased P99 latency for small requests (explainable by extra syncs).
hypotheses: H1: KV prefetch completes on an auxiliary stream then frees on a different stream without stream-ordered frees; cudaMallocAsync's deferred freeing defers page return until stream completion, creating temporary multi-arena residency.
H2: Large number of small ephemeral allocations from subcomponents (tokenizers, small temporary tensors in runtime) prevent effective slab coalescing and cause arena proliferation.

H3: The allocator's threshold for returning unused arenas to the OS/device is too conservative for mixed small/medium workloads; tuning heuristics can reduce resident spikes without requiring full synchronization.

H4: A lightweight handoff protocol (KV-cache handshake) that ensures frees are performed on the same stream or uses explicit stream synchronization at prefetch boundaries will reduce hold time for pages.
H5: Batched free/defragmentation windows (periodic coalescer that runs off the critical path) can reclaim small fragments into larger free extents with bounded latency impact.

H6: Using host-staging for prefetched KV (keep device allocation shorter) can reduce device fragmentation at the cost of higher host-device transfer bandwidth; this tradeoff may be acceptable for some customers.
Primary mitigation should avoid adding synchronous stalls to the happy path.
experiments_run: E1: Disable KV prefetch in the repro: resident spike amplitude reduced by 55% but end-to-end throughput dropped for large request patterns.
E2: Force frees to occur on the same stream as allocation (instrumentation patch): spikes mitigated but introduced a 0.8% P95 latency increase for medium batches due to extra stream ordering fences.
E3: Implemented aggressive arena-return heuristic in debug build (return arenas after N seconds idle): baseline recovery improved but increased cudaMallocAsync overhead observed under bursty traffic.
E4: Batched-defrag worker that coalesces small frees into larger extents off the critical path: improved resident baseline with negligible latency impact when tuned to low frequency (30s).

E5: Host-staging for KV prefetch (prefetch into pinned host memory then async copy to device at reuse time): reduced device arena churn but increased host bandwidth and slightly higher latency on first-use of prefetched KV.
E6: Combined E2 (stream-handshake) with E4 (defrag worker) in a staging build: best trade-off so far—spikes reduced ~80%, P99 latency change within acceptable bounds for dedicated-tier SLAs.
Logs and dashboards for each experiment stored in Confluence page and grafana runbooks (links below).
decisions: Short-term: backport a minimal stream-handshake patch to ensure KV prefetch frees happen on the allocation stream when feasible (non-blocking). This is a low-risk change to reduce peak resident spikes.

Medium-term: upstream an allocator enhancement: a background batched-defrag worker that coalesces freed blocks across arenas with configurable frequency and budget. Default disabled for hosted tier; enabled for Dedicated customers via runtime flag.
Long-term: evaluate host-staging + on-demand device promotion for KV cache as a tunable policy per-customer workload profile in runtime-1.24.
We will avoid immediate addition of synchronous device fences on the critical path; prefer background or handshakes that preserve throughput.
Assign release window for the short-term patch to runtime-1.22 as hotfix for customers experiencing resident drift.
Add runtime metrics: allocator.fragmentation_index, allocator.arena_count, kv.prefetch_stream_mismatch_rate to help monitor in production.
next_steps: 1) Create PR for stream-handshake patch (ENG-526301-PR) and request eng-runtime review. Target: small, well-documented change with feature flag.
2) Add unit + integration tests that simulate cross-stream alloc/free sequences and validate no regressions in throughput.
3) Instrument a canary in dedicated pool with the patch enabled for 48h; collect nvml traces and grafana dashboards.
4) Prototype background batched-defrag worker and run internal experiments to select safe defaults (frequency=30s, cpu-budget=5%).
5) Update runbook: steps for diagnosing resident spikes and temporary mitigations (toggle prefetch, enable defrag worker).
6) Schedule a post-mortem if customer incidents occur during rollout and prepare communication for enterprises on runtime-1.22 release notes.
7) Link to storage: confluence://runtime/memory/ENG-526301 and gh://redwood/runtime/pulls/526301 (draft).
notes: Reviewers: please pay attention to potential perf regressions for small-batch P95 when enabling stream synchronization.
Consider exposing defrag worker as an opt-in runtime tunable for Dedicated customers first to gather telemetry before enabling broadly.
Follow-on: check interaction with kernel scheduler changes in runtime-1.21 that altered stream priorities; could exacerbate delayed free completion windows.
If we find production signals of similar resident growth in hosted customers, escalate to SRE for emergency canary rollout controls.
Assign a cross-team review with Console for new allocator metrics to ensure visible SLO impact in dashboards.
